set1.q: A 69-year-old man has sudden severe pain in his right leg. Pulses are absent below the knee. Which examination finding is often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency?
opts: Sensory loss over the foot's dorsum

Correct. His sudden severe pain with absent pulses below the knee is acute limb ischemia. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so sensory deficits over the dorsum of the foot are often the earliest neurologic sign of acute vascular insufficiency, which is why sensory testing is part of the examination.
Complete paralysis of the leg

Paralysis is a late finding; profound weakness with paralysis marks an irreversibly ischemic limb. The earliest neurologic sign is sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot, because light-touch fibers are most susceptible to ischemia. Early is sensory, late is motor.
Absent patellar reflex

Reflex testing is not named as the early sign. Light-touch sensory fibers are highly susceptible to ischemia, so loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot comes earliest. The examination emphasizes sensory and muscle strength testing.
Loss of hair on the shin

Hair loss is a chronic sign of peripheral artery disease, part of the loss of dermal appendages from long-standing poor flow, not a neurologic sign. In his sudden ischemia, the earliest neurologic sign is sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Chronic skin changes do not appear in hours.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man has a 3.1 cm femoral pseudoaneurysm that has persisted since his catheterization. Which treatment seals the leak?
opts: Catheter-directed thrombolysis

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves clot in acute limb ischemia of under 14 days, the opposite of what a pseudoaneurysm needs. A pseudoaneurysm is sealed by promoting clot, with ultrasound-guided thrombin injection. Lysis would keep the leak open.
Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection

Correct. His pseudoaneurysm is 3.1 cm, larger than the under-2 cm size that may thrombose and regress spontaneously, and it has persisted. Ultrasound-guided injection of thrombin, which promotes clot, seals the leak. Watch and wait is reserved for those under 2 cm.
Watch and wait

Watchful waiting is for pseudoaneurysms under 2 cm, which may undergo spontaneous thrombosis and regression. His is 3.1 cm and has persisted since catheterization, so the leak should be sealed with ultrasound-guided thrombin. Size over 2 cm and persistence both argue against waiting.
Intravenous heparin
Heparin prevents the clotting that seals a pseudoaneurysm cavity. The leak is sealed by ultrasound-guided thrombin injection, which promotes clot. Anticoagulation works against the treatment goal.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with sudden leg ischemia has sensory loss extending beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal. Where should his evaluation and treatment take place?
opts: Nowhere; plan major amputation

Major amputation is for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous Doppler signals. His venous signal is audible and his weakness only mild to moderate, so the limb is immediately threatened and still salvageable with immediate revascularization.
In the surgical suite, without delay

Correct. Sensory loss beyond the toes with rest pain, mild-to-moderate weakness, an inaudible arterial Doppler signal and an audible venous signal define an immediately threatened limb. It is salvageable with immediate revascularization, so it should preferentially undergo further evaluation and treatment in a surgical suite.
After outpatient duplex imaging

Outpatient testing wastes time this limb does not have. Sensory loss beyond the toes with mild-to-moderate weakness means an immediately threatened limb, salvageable only with immediate revascularization in a surgical suite. Outpatient pathways belong to chronic disease.
After computed tomography first

Sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography belongs to viable and marginally threatened limbs, which have no sensory loss or weakness. His deficits make the limb immediately threatened, so evaluation and treatment belong in the surgical suite. His weakness removes the time for imaging.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and an acute dissection has had his systolic pressure lowered to 110 mmHg and his pain controlled. Which definitive treatment removes the diseased segment?
opts: Surgical grafting of the aorta

Correct. With his systolic pressure at 110 mmHg, inside the 100 to 120 mmHg target, and his pain controlled, the definitive step is surgery: grafting and replacing the diseased portion of the aorta. Blood pressure reduction stops progression, but only the graft removes the diseased segment.
Catheter-directed thrombolysis

Catheter-directed thrombolysis dissolves arterial clot in acute limb ischemia of under 14 days. A dissection is a torn aortic wall, not a clot, and is definitively treated by grafting and replacing the diseased aorta. Lysis has no role in a dissection.
Ultrasound-guided thrombin

Ultrasound-guided thrombin injection seals the leak of a pseudoaneurysm by promoting clot. A dissection needs the diseased aorta surgically grafted and replaced. Thrombin treats a small cavity outside an artery, not a dissected aorta.
Carotid endarterectomy

Carotid endarterectomy removes plaque from the carotid artery and is the gold standard for high-grade carotid stenosis. A dissected aorta is repaired by grafting and replacing the diseased portion. The procedure must match the vessel and the lesion.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with a 4.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm has a history of severe reaction to contrast dye. She is stable, and the extent of the aneurysm must be defined. Which imaging is most appropriate?
opts: Conventional angiography

Conventional angiography requires contrast injected through a catheter, which her severe dye reaction rules against. For a stable patient with a dye allergy, magnetic resonance imaging defines the aneurysm without dye or ionizing radiation. Any contrast-based study is the wrong choice for her.
Magnetic resonance imaging

Correct. Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without exposure to dye or ionizing radiation, which makes it useful in stable patients with a dye allergy. She is stable, her severe contrast reaction rules out dye-based studies, and the extent of her 4.8 cm aneurysm can still be defined.
Computed tomography angiography

Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, but it relies on contrast dye, and she has had a severe reaction. Magnetic resonance imaging gives comparable information without dye. Her allergy is the clue that moves the choice.
Abdominal X-ray

A plain film shows only a calcified outline, in about 75% of aneurysms, and misses the 25% that are not calcified. It cannot define extent. Magnetic resonance imaging can, without dye, which suits her allergy.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man has an incidental 4.0 cm ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm on a chest radiograph and follow-up imaging. He has no symptoms. Which surveillance plan is appropriate?
opts: Abdominal ultrasound every three years with no other imaging

Three-yearly ultrasound is the plan for small abdominal aortic aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm, not the thoracic aorta. His ascending thoracic aneurysm is followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Abdominal surveillance does not image the chest.
Open repair with aortic root replacement within the month

Asymptomatic ascending repair is generally indicated above 5.5 cm or with growth over 0.5 cm per year. At 4.0 cm with no symptoms he needs surveillance, not surgery. Open repair with root replacement is the method once repair is indicated, not the plan now.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 3 to 5 years

Correct. A root, ascending or descending thoracic aneurysm under 4.5 cm is followed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging every 3 to 5 years. His 4.0 cm ascending aneurysm is asymptomatic and below every repair trigger, so this interval applies.
Computed tomography or magnetic resonance every 6 to 12 months

Imaging every 6 to 12 months applies to thoracic aneurysms of 4.5 to 5.4 cm. At 4.0 cm, his aneurysm is below 4.5 cm, so the interval is every 3 to 5 years. Check which side of 4.5 cm the measurement falls.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension reports calf pain after walking about two blocks that resolves with rest. His ankle-brachial index is 0.62 on the left and normal on the right. Which interpretation fits the left-sided value?
opts: Rest pain and tissue loss range

Rest pain and tissue loss, ulcer or gangrene, correspond to an ankle-brachial index of 0 to 0.4. His left value of 0.62 is higher, and his symptom is exertional calf pain relieved by rest, not rest pain. Both the number and the history fit claudication.
Noncompressible artery range

An index above 1.3 is abnormal and reflects calcified, noncompressible arteries, as in a diabetic patient. His left value of 0.62 is genuinely reduced and falls in the claudication band. Noncompressible arteries give high readings, not low ones.
Claudication range

Correct. An ankle-brachial index of 0.4 to 0.9 is the claudication range, and his left value of 0.62 sits within it. It matches his calf pain after walking two blocks that resolves with rest, while his normal right side lies above 0.9 up to 1.3.
Normal range

A normal ankle-brachial index lies above 0.9 up to 1.3, which describes his right side. His left value of 0.62 is reduced and falls in the claudication band of 0.4 to 0.9, matching his exertional calf pain. Normal requires a value above 0.9.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man has had a cold, pulseless right leg for three hours, with pallor, tingling and mild weakness of the toes. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Immediate vascular surgery consult

Correct. A cold, pulseless leg for three hours with pallor, tingling and toe weakness is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency, and weakness places it at least in the immediately threatened category. Management begins with an immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin, with testing guided by the category of ischemia.
Outpatient ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for chronic peripheral artery disease in a stable patient. A sudden cold, pulseless leg with sensory and motor changes is a vascular emergency needing an immediate vascular surgery consult. Clinic testing would waste critical time.
Supervised exercise referral

Supervised exercise improves walking distance in stable claudication. His cold, pale, pulseless leg with tingling and weakness for three hours is acute limb ischemia, which needs an immediate vascular surgery consult. Exercise has no role in an acute occlusion.
Start cilostazol and follow up

Cilostazol is an oral antiplatelet and vasodilator for chronic claudication. An acute occlusion with pallor, tingling and weakness needs an immediate vascular surgery consult and intravenous heparin, not an oral drug with follow-up. Delay risks the limb.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man who smokes a pack a day has calf claudication and an ankle-brachial index of 0.7. He asks what matters most for his legs. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Stop smoking completely

Correct. Cigarette smoking carries three times the risk of peripheral artery disease compared with nonsmokers, and smoking cessation leads the list of risk-factor reduction measures in medical management. For a pack-a-day smoker with claudication and an index of 0.7, quitting completely matters most.
Limit walking to avoid pain

Consistent moderate exercise improves walking distance in claudication, so limiting walking works against him. Exercise therapy, at least 30 to 45 minutes three times a week, is part of management. For a pack-a-day smoker, complete smoking cessation is the most important counseling point.
Elevate the legs when painful

Elevating the leg removes gravity's help to arterial flow and worsens ischemic pain, as in the rest pain of critical limb ischemia. His priority as a pack-a-day smoker with claudication is complete smoking cessation. Elevation is the wrong direction for an ischemic leg.
Switch to occasional cigars

Switching to occasional cigars is still tobacco use, while the risk-reduction measure is smoking cessation. Cigarette smoking triples the risk of peripheral artery disease compared with nonsmokers. The counseling goal is quitting completely, not changing the product.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man has pain in both legs when walking, with numbness and weakness. Standing still does not help; the pain eases only when he sits down or leans forward over a shopping cart. His pedal pulses are normal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Spinal stenosis

Correct. Walking-induced pain in both legs with numbness and weakness, not relieved by standing still but eased by sitting or leaning forward over a cart, is spinal stenosis. It is relieved by rest and by sitting down or leaning forward to straighten out the lumbar spine, and his normal pedal pulses argue against arterial disease.
Peripheral artery disease

Arterial claudication is relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes, so standing still would ease it, and pulses are diminished or absent below the stenosis. His pulses are normal and only sitting or leaning forward helps. Those two clues point to spinal stenosis.
Peripheral neuropathy

Peripheral neuropathy causes a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. His pain is triggered by walking and relieved by sitting or leaning forward. Exercise-linked, posture-relieved pain is not neuropathy.
Venous insufficiency

Venous insufficiency causes swelling and discomfort in the calf with standing, with swelling made worse by prolonged walking. He has no swelling, and his numbness, weakness and relief with leaning forward fit spinal stenosis. Swelling is the missing venous clue.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden, severe, ripping chest pain. His electrocardiogram is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Computed tomography, chest and abdomen

Correct. Sudden, severe, ripping chest pain in a man with hypertension is the presentation of aortic dissection, and the electrocardiogram may be normal in dissection, so his normal tracing does not exclude it. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent of the dissection.
Reassure him; the tracing is normal

A normal electrocardiogram does not rule out aortic dissection, in which the tracing may be normal. Sudden ripping chest pain in a man with hypertension needs computed tomography of the chest and abdomen. Reassurance on a normal tracing is the classic error here.
Ankle-brachial index measurement

The ankle-brachial index grades lower extremity arterial disease and says nothing about chest pain. Suspected dissection is imaged with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen, or with magnetic resonance imaging or transesophageal echocardiography. Match the test to the vessel at risk.
Abdominal plain radiograph

A plain abdominal film is not among the studies for aortic dissection and cannot show its extent. Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen delineates the extent; magnetic resonance imaging and transesophageal echocardiography are alternatives. His ripping chest pain needs cross-sectional imaging.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man who smokes and has diabetes reports aching in both buttocks and hips after walking two blocks, relieved by about 10 minutes of rest. He also reports erectile dysfunction. Both femoral pulses are diminished. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tibial artery disease

Tibial disease produces foot claudication, at the far end of the leg, and does not explain weak femoral pulses. His buttock and hip pain, erectile dysfunction and diminished femoral pulses all point to the aortoiliac segment. The pain site maps to the level of the lesion.
Aortoiliac occlusive disease

Correct. Buttock and hip claudication points to aortoiliac disease, which can diminish one or both femoral pulses and, when severe, causes erectile dysfunction. Claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction together form the Leriche syndrome triad, and he has all three.
Superficial femoral artery disease

Superficial femoral artery stenosis causes claudication in the upper two-thirds of the calf, the most common site. His pain is in the buttocks and hips with diminished femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction, which places the lesion higher, in the aortoiliac segment. Calf pain would point lower.
Lumbar spinal stenosis

Spinal stenosis gives claudication-like symptoms with numbness and weakness, relieved by sitting down or leaning forward, and does not explain weak femoral pulses. His pain eases with rest alone, his femoral pulses are diminished and he has erectile dysfunction, the Leriche triad of aortoiliac disease.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man presents with painful blue toes and palpable pedal pulses. On abdominal examination there is a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. Which lesion is the likely source of his emboli?
opts: Carotid artery plaque

Carotid plaque is linked to atheroembolization and stroke, and a neck lesion would not explain a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus. His painful blue toes, palpable pedal pulses and pulsatile abdominal mass point to an abdominal aortic aneurysm with embolic phenomena. The mass locates the source.
Femoral pseudoaneurysm

A femoral pseudoaneurysm follows catheterization and causes local groin pain from swelling or nerve compression. His mass is pulsatile and abdominal, above the umbilicus, which points to an abdominal aortic aneurysm shedding emboli to the toes. The location of the mass is the clue.
Thoracic aortic dissection

Aortic dissection forms from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen within the media, not an abdominal pulsatile mass with emboli. His pulsatile mass above the umbilicus with painful blue toes is an abdominal aortic aneurysm with embolic phenomena (blue toe syndrome). Tell: the mass is in the abdomen, not the thorax.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm

Correct. A symptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm can produce embolic phenomena that lead to blue toe syndrome. His pulsatile mass above the umbilicus is the aneurysm, and painful blue toes with palpable pedal pulses fit small emboli lodging in the digits rather than a large-artery occlusion.

set1.q: A 65-year-old woman has a suddenly cool left foot with mild toe pain. She has no sensory loss and no muscle weakness, and venous Doppler signals are present. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Computed tomography angiography

Correct. A suddenly cool foot with mild toe pain, no sensory loss, no weakness and audible venous Doppler signals is a viable or marginally threatened limb. Both categories have sufficient time for vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography before treatment, which makes it the next step here.
Immediate major amputation

Major amputation is for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss, paralysis and inaudible arterial and venous signals. Her limb has no neurologic deficit and an audible venous signal, so there is time to image it first. Nothing here suggests an unsalvageable limb.
Direct transfer to the surgical suite

Immediately threatened limbs, with sensory loss beyond the toes, rest pain and mild-to-moderate weakness, go straight to the surgical suite. She has no sensory loss or weakness, so there is sufficient time for imaging first. Deficits are what take away imaging time.
Discharge with oral aspirin

A suddenly cool foot is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency even without deficits; her limb is salvageable if treated promptly, not safe to send home. The next step is vascular imaging such as computed tomography angiography. Oral aspirin alone does not answer an acute occlusion.

set1.q: A 68-year-old man with a 5.9 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is being prepared for repair. Which study is best for diagnosis and pre-intervention planning?
opts: Abdominal X-ray

A plain film may show a calcified outline in about 75% of aneurysms but cannot define location, size and extent for repair. His 5.9 cm aneurysm is being prepared for repair, which calls for computed tomography angiography. An outline is not a surgical map.
Transesophageal echocardiography

Transesophageal echocardiography evaluates the aortic valve and aortic root in thoracic disease and does not image an abdominal aneurysm. His repair is planned with computed tomography angiography, the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study. The probe looks at the wrong segment.
Computed tomography angiography

Correct. Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, accurately delineating the location, size and extent of the aneurysm. For a 5.9 cm aneurysm already being prepared for repair, that anatomical detail is what the surgeon needs.
Abdominal ultrasound

Ultrasound is the study of choice for initial screening and serial documentation of aneurysm size, not for planning repair. Once his 5.9 cm aneurysm is headed for repair, computed tomography angiography is the best pre-intervention study. Screening and planning are different jobs.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man with extensive atherosclerosis develops painful, tender, bluish discoloration of several toes on his left foot, with localized pallor. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute embolic limb ischemia

A thromboembolus occluding a limb artery produces a cold, pale limb with absent pulses distal to the occlusion. His dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable, with tender blue toes, which points to atheroembolism. Palpable pulses argue against a large-artery occlusion.
Critical limb ischemia

Critical limb ischemia is chronic rest pain, ulcers and tissue loss with diminished pulses below the stenosis. His tender, bluish toes with easily palpable pulses fit atheroembolism instead. Preserved pulses separate small-vessel emboli from chronic large-vessel disease.
Dry gangrene

Dry gangrene is hard, dry, necrotic tissue with clear demarcation between healthy and dead tissue. His toes are tender and bluish with localized pallor, not black and demarcated. Gangrene may develop later, but the current picture is atheroembolism.
Atheroembolism

Correct. Atheroemboli of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol debris from proximal plaques lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin, causing blue toe syndrome with localized tenderness, pallor and livedo reticularis. Because large vessels may not be occluded, distal pulses usually remain palpable, as his are.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man has constant hypogastric and low back pain for two days. A tender pulsatile mass is felt; blood pressure is 152/90 and stable. Imaging shows a 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm without rupture. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Discharge with smoking advice

Smoking cessation is part of long-term management, but his constant pain and tender 5.8 cm unruptured aneurysm make it symptomatic. A symptomatic unruptured aneurysm needs blood pressure control with beta blockers and surgical repair unless contraindicated. He cannot be sent home.
Refer once it reaches 6.5 cm

A painful aneurysm needs urgent referral regardless of size, and his already measures 5.8 cm. A symptomatic unruptured aneurysm is managed with pain control, blood pressure control with beta blockers and surgical repair. There is no 6.5 cm threshold to wait for.
Beta blocker and surgical repair

Correct. Two days of hypogastric and low back pain with a tender pulsatile mass and stable pressure is a symptomatic, unruptured aneurysm. Management is to evaluate hemodynamic stability, place large-bore intravenous catheters, control pain, control blood pressure with beta blockers and perform surgical repair unless contraindicated.
Ultrasound again in six months

Surveillance imaging is for asymptomatic aneurysms. His constant pain with a tender pulsatile mass makes the aneurysm symptomatic, which calls for beta blocker therapy and surgical repair now. Pain ends the surveillance pathway.

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman has constant throbbing, burning pain in her toes and forefoot that is worse lying flat, not relieved by narcotic pain medicine, and eased by dangling her leg or walking around. Her feet are cool. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Peripheral neuropathy

Peripheral neuropathy gives a continuous burning sensation in the foot that is unaffected by exercise. Her pain is worse lying flat and eased by dangling or walking, and her feet are cool, which is arterial rest pain. Position dependence points to ischemia.
Acute limb ischemia

Acute limb ischemia is a sudden occlusion with abrupt onset of severe pain and absent pulses, a vascular emergency. Her constant pain that worsens lying flat and eases with dangling is the established pattern of critical limb ischemia. Nothing in the stem describes an abrupt onset.
Critical limb ischemia

Correct. Ischemic rest pain of critical limb ischemia is constant, throbbing or burning, in the forefoot and toes, with cool feet. It worsens with elevation or reclining, is not readily controlled even by narcotics, and is relieved by dependency or walking around, which use gravity to aid perfusion.

Claudication is activity-related muscle pain relieved by rest, usually in about 10 minutes. Her pain is constant, worse lying flat and eased by walking or dangling, which is ischemic rest pain. Walking relieves her pain, whereas claudication is caused by it.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with hypertension has a carotid bruit found on routine examination. She has never had neurologic symptoms. Duplex shows 35% stenosis. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Digital subtraction angiography

Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard used to guide therapeutic interventions, and none is indicated for her. Her 35% stenosis is low grade, under 50%, and is managed medically. An invasive study has no role when no intervention is planned.
Medical management

Correct. Medical management is advised for symptomatic and asymptomatic patients with low-grade stenosis under 50%, and hers is 35% without symptoms. It includes antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin or clopidogrel, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, smoking cessation, healthy diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Carotid endarterectomy

Endarterectomy is advised for symptomatic stenosis over 70% or asymptomatic stenosis over 80% with a life expectancy over five years. Her 35% asymptomatic stenosis is far below either threshold and is managed medically. A bruit alone does not trigger surgery.
Carotid stenting

Carotid stenting is a less invasive revascularization for poor surgical candidates who need intervention. Her 35% asymptomatic stenosis needs no intervention at all, since under 50% is managed medically. Stenting changes the route, not the indication.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man arrives with a suddenly cold, pale, pulseless left foot. Vascular surgery has been called. Which medical therapy should be started?
opts: Cilostazol

Cilostazol is an oral drug that suppresses platelet aggregation and dilates vessels to improve walking distance in chronic claudication. A suddenly cold, pale, pulseless foot is acute limb ischemia, anticoagulated with intravenous heparin while vascular surgery acts. Chronic drugs do not treat acute occlusion.
Pentoxifylline

Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative that helps blood flow through narrowed arteries in chronic disease. Acute arterial occlusion needs intravenous heparin anticoagulation alongside the vascular surgery consult. An oral chronic agent does not fit this emergency.
Intravenous heparin

Correct. A suddenly cold, pale, pulseless foot is acute peripheral arterial occlusion, and its medical therapy is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin, started alongside the immediate vascular surgery consult. Diagnostic testing then depends on the category of ischemia.
Oral aspirin alone

Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent used in chronic peripheral artery disease. The medical therapy for an acute arterial occlusion is anticoagulation with intravenous heparin. An oral antiplatelet alone is not the acute treatment.

set1.q: A 72-year-old woman with a femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterization reports increasing thigh pain and tingling around the swelling. Which explains her pain?
opts: Retroperitoneal rupture of the aorta

Retroperitoneal bleeding is the picture of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, with severe abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile mass and hypotension. Her pain and tingling sit around a femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterization, which fits swelling and nerve compression. The pain is local, not central.
Critical limb ischemia rest pain

Ischemic rest pain is constant pain in the forefoot and toes, worse on elevation and relieved by dependency. Her pain is in the thigh around the pseudoaneurysm swelling, with tingling, which reflects swelling pressure and nerve compression. Location around the swelling is the clue.
Atheroemboli to the toes

Atheroemboli cause painful blue toes, not pain and tingling around a groin swelling. A pseudoaneurysm causes pain from increased pressure due to swelling or from nerve compression. Her symptoms sit at the swelling, not in the digits.
Swelling and nerve compression

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm presents with pain due to increased pressure from swelling or from nerve compression. Her increasing thigh pain with tingling around the swelling after femoral catheterization matches both mechanisms, the tingling pointing to a compressed nerve.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man who smokes and has hypertension had a transient ischemic attack four months ago: weakness of his left arm that fully cleared within an hour. A right carotid bruit is heard, and duplex ultrasonography shows significant stenosis. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Asymptomatic carotid artery disease

Asymptomatic carotid disease means significant stenosis with no ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack within the last six months. His attack four months ago falls inside that window, so he is symptomatic. Resolution within an hour does not make him asymptomatic.
Thoracic aortic aneurysm

Thoracic aortic aneurysms are mostly asymptomatic or cause aortic regurgitation, hoarseness or compression symptoms depending on location. A transient ischemic attack with a carotid bruit and stenosis on duplex is carotid disease. His findings localize to the neck, not the chest.
Aortic dissection

Aortic dissection forms from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen within the media. A brief episode of arm weakness with a carotid bruit and stenosis on duplex points to symptomatic carotid disease. Tell: a transient focal neurologic deficit plus carotid stenosis points to the carotid, not the aorta.
Symptomatic carotid artery disease

Correct. A transient ischemic attack (a focal loss of neurologic function lasting less than 24 hours) within the last six months makes carotid disease symptomatic. His left arm weakness cleared within an hour four months ago, and he has a right carotid bruit and significant stenosis on duplex.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman being treated for an acute aortic dissection develops a new diastolic murmur and worsening breathlessness. Which complication explains these findings?
opts: Aortic regurgitation

Correct. Aortic dissection can cause aortic regurgitation through dilatation of the aortic root, alongside its other presenting features of tearing chest pain, syncope and hypertension or hypotension. A new diastolic murmur with worsening breathlessness during treatment for a dissection fits that complication.
Mitral stenosis

Mitral stenosis is not a listed consequence of aortic dissection. The valve affected in dissection is the aortic valve, through dilatation of the aortic root, producing aortic regurgitation. The anatomy points to the aortic root, not the mitral valve.
Pseudoaneurysm

A pseudoaneurysm is a blood-filled cavity outside an arterial wall, usually the femoral artery after catheterization, causing local pain from swelling or nerve compression. It does not cause a new murmur. Her diastolic murmur reflects aortic regurgitation from root dilatation.
Carotid stenosis

Carotid stenosis is an atherosclerotic narrowing that can produce a bruit and neurologic symptoms, not a diastolic murmur with breathlessness. In dissection, dilatation of the aortic root causes aortic regurgitation. Her findings are cardiac, not neurologic.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with claudication and an ankle-brachial index of 0.72 has no bleeding history. Which medication class should be started to lower his risk of myocardial infarction and stroke?
opts: Intravenous heparin

Intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion, not chronic claudication. To lower the risk of myocardial infarction and stroke in stable peripheral artery disease, an antiplatelet agent is started. Acute anticoagulation answers a different problem.
A loop diuretic

A diuretic has no listed role in peripheral artery disease. Antiplatelet agents, aspirin, clopidogrel or cilostazol, decrease the overall risk of cardiovascular disease from myocardial infarction and stroke and improve walking distance. Fluid management is not the risk reduction asked about.
An antiplatelet agent

Correct. Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel or cilostazol decreases the overall risk of cardiovascular disease from myocardial infarction and stroke and improves walking distance by enhancing circulation. With claudication, an index of 0.72 and no bleeding history, he is a clear candidate.
A thrombolytic agent

Thrombolytic agents, such as alteplase given by catheter, are for acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days. Stable claudication with an index of 0.72 is chronic disease, and the class that lowers infarction and stroke risk is an antiplatelet agent. Clot dissolution is an acute therapy.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with a known 4.2 cm thoracic aortic aneurysm comes to urgent care with new chest and back pain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Routine imaging in six months

Scheduled surveillance is for asymptomatic aneurysms; at 4.2 cm hers would be imaged every 3 to 5 years. New chest and back pain with a known thoracic aneurysm requires urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause. Symptoms override the routine schedule.
Reassurance and pain relief

Treating the pain without imaging risks missing an aneurysm that has become symptomatic. Chest or back pain with a known thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause, and all symptomatic thoracic aneurysms are repaired. Imaging comes first.
Ankle-brachial index today

The ankle-brachial index assesses leg arteries and cannot explain chest and back pain. A known thoracic aneurysm with new pain needs urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause. The test must look at the thoracic aorta.
Urgent imaging of the aorta

Correct. Chest or back pain with a known or suspected thoracic aortic aneurysm must undergo urgent imaging to rule out the aneurysm as the cause. Her new pain with a known 4.2 cm aneurysm fits exactly, and if the aneurysm is the cause, repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man who had a large anterior myocardial infarction three weeks ago develops sudden pain and coldness of his right leg with absent foot pulses. Which cardiac finding is the most likely embolic source?
opts: A calcified mitral leaflet

Valve calcification is not a named embolic source. After his large myocardial infarction three weeks ago, a left ventricular thrombus is the classic origin of an embolus to the leg. The heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, through clot rather than calcium.
A pericardial effusion

Fluid around the heart is not an embolic source. The cardiac sources named for limb emboli are atrial fibrillation and left ventricular thrombus after a myocardial infarction. His recent large infarction points to a ventricular clot.
An atrial septal scar

A septal scar is not a recognized embolic source here. After a myocardial infarction, a left ventricular thrombus can dislodge, travel distally and occlude a smaller artery. His three-week-old anterior infarction makes the ventricle the likely source.
Left ventricular thrombus

Correct. Thromboemboli are the most common emboli in acute limb ischemia, and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, for example atrial fibrillation or a left ventricular thrombus after a myocardial infarction. His large anterior infarction three weeks ago makes a ventricular thrombus the likely source.

set1.q: A 60-year-old man with carotid artery disease on duplex smokes a pack a day and asks whether quitting still matters now that he takes aspirin. Which counseling point is accurate?
opts: Smoking harms only the leg arteries

Smoking is not a leg-only risk; in carotid artery disease it nearly doubles the risk of stroke, and smoking cessation is part of medical management. His aspirin does not change that. Carotid disease has its own smoking statistic.
Smoking nearly doubles stroke risk

Correct. Smoking nearly doubles the risk of stroke, so smoking cessation is part of the medical management of carotid artery disease. It sits alongside antiplatelet therapy such as his aspirin, control of hypertension, diabetes and lipids, healthy diet, exercise and weight reduction.
Aspirin cancels the smoking risk

Antiplatelet therapy and smoking cessation are separate parts of carotid disease management; aspirin does not cancel the smoking risk. Smoking nearly doubles the risk of stroke, so he still needs to quit. Both measures are needed together.
Quitting only matters before surgery

Smoking cessation is part of medical management for carotid disease in every patient, surgical or not, because smoking nearly doubles the risk of stroke. He should quit now, whatever his surgical plan. Cessation is not only a preoperative step.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with claudication, a known contrast allergy and reduced renal function needs arterial imaging before a planned intervention. Which study is relatively contraindicated for her?
opts: Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test that uses no contrast, so neither her allergy nor her kidneys limit it. It is the important initial test, but it does not image anatomy for intervention. It is not the study with a contraindication for her.
Computed tomography angiography

Correct. Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to delineate arterial anatomy, and its listed contraindications are contrast allergy and decreased renal function. She has both, so it is the study to avoid; magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative in contrast allergy.
Magnetic resonance angiography

Magnetic resonance angiography is the alternative for patients with a contrast allergy. Its listed contraindications are pacemakers and intracranial aneurysm clips, which she does not have. Her allergy and kidneys point away from the contrast study, not this one.
Duplex ultrasound

Duplex ultrasound is noninvasive and uses no contrast media or radiation, so it is safe with her allergy and kidney function. It is the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging when stenosis is suspected. No contrast means no conflict here.

set1.q: A 75-year-old man with peripheral artery disease has a hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue. There is no swelling, moisture or fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atheroembolism

Atheroembolism causes painful, tender blue toes with pallor and livedo reticularis, usually with palpable pulses. A hard, dry, black distal toe with a clear line between healthy and dead tissue is dry gangrene. Blue and tender differs from black and hard.
Dry gangrene

Correct. Dry gangrene has a hard, dry texture, usually involves the distal toes, shows clear demarcation between healthy and necrotic tissue, and is common in patients with peripheral artery disease. His toe matches every feature, with no swelling, moisture or fever to suggest infection.
Wet gangrene

Wet gangrene has a moist appearance, edema and blistering, with bacterial infection and a risk of sepsis, and it is a surgical emergency. His toe is hard and dry with no swelling, moisture or fever. The absence of moisture and fever separates dry from wet.
Gas gangrene

Gas gangrene is a wet gangrene in which spore-forming clostridial species release toxins and gas into infected tissue. His dry, clearly demarcated toe without swelling, moisture or fever is dry gangrene. Gas gangrene sits on the wet, infected side.

opts: Digital subtraction angiography

Digital subtraction angiography is the invasive gold standard, but it is not used for screening; it guides therapeutic interventions. Her first carotid test after a transient episode and a bruit is duplex ultrasonography. Gold standard and first test are different roles.
Computed tomography of the chest

Chest computed tomography is not among the carotid studies; carotid evaluation uses duplex ultrasonography first, then computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the cervical and intracranial vessels. Her symptoms and bruit call for duplex. A chest scan misses the neck.
Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is the initial test for peripheral artery disease in the legs. Her transient right arm weakness and slurred speech with a left carotid bruit need carotid imaging, starting with duplex ultrasonography. A leg test does not evaluate the carotids.
Duplex ultrasonography

Correct. Her 20-minute episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved, with a left carotid bruit, points to carotid disease. Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening tool and is also used to monitor patients serially for progression or after intervention.

For this man being prepared for intervention, digital subtraction angiography, the invasive gold standard, guides therapy. Effective imaging is not the reference test.
Carotid auscultation for a bruit

A bruit is an examination finding, auscultated one side at a time with the breath held, not an imaging study. It cannot define his stenosis for intervention; digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard used to guide therapeutic interventions. An examination sign is not a test standard.
Digital subtraction angiography

Correct. Digital subtraction angiography is an invasive angiographic technique considered the gold standard for carotid artery disease. It is not used for screening but for guiding therapeutic interventions, which fits a man whose high-grade stenosis after a transient ischemic attack is already headed for intervention.
Duplex ultrasonography

Duplex ultrasonography is the most widely used initial screening tool, and it already found his high-grade stenosis; it is also used for serial monitoring. The gold standard, used to guide intervention, is digital subtraction angiography. Duplex screens and follows; angiography guides treatment.

set2.q: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who takes no anticoagulant develops sudden, severe pain in her left leg two hours ago. The leg is cold and pale, pulses are absent below the femoral artery, and she has numbness over the dorsum of the foot. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Critical limb ischemia

Critical limb ischemia is chronic: constant rest pain in the forefoot and toes and nonhealing ulcers that build over time. Her pain began two hours ago in a previously normal leg, with a cold, pale, pulseless limb and untreated atrial fibrillation. Abrupt onset points to acute embolic occlusion.
Atheroembolism with blue toes

Atheroemboli lodge in small vessels of skin and muscle, so distal pulses usually stay palpable while the toes turn blue. Her pulses are absent below the femoral artery and the whole leg is cold and pale, which means a larger artery is occluded. Absent pulses argue against atheroembolism.
Intermittent claudication

Claudication is predictable exertional pain relieved by rest, usually within 10 minutes. Her pain began suddenly two hours ago with a cold, pale, pulseless leg and numbness over the dorsum of the foot. That is acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency, not chronic exertional pain.
Acute embolic limb ischemia

Correct. Sudden severe pain with a cold, pale leg and absent pulses below the femoral artery is acute limb ischemia, sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery. Thromboemboli are most common and the heart is the source in 80 to 90% of cases, with atrial fibrillation a named source; numbness over the dorsum of the foot is an early neurologic sign.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman who smokes has cramping in her right calf after walking one block that eases after she stands still for several minutes. Her pedal pulses are diminished on the right. Which is the best initial test?
opts: Magnetic resonance angiography

Magnetic resonance angiography is an alternative to computed tomography angiography in contrast allergy and, like it, is used mainly to guide a planned intervention. Her suspected peripheral artery disease starts with the bedside ankle-brachial index. Anatomy studies come after the diagnosis is established.
Ankle-brachial index

Correct. Calf cramping after one block that eases with standing still, plus diminished right pedal pulses in a smoker, is classic claudication. The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test and the important initial test, with 0.4 to 0.9 the claudication band; it divides the higher ankle pressure by the higher arm pressure.
Conventional angiography

Conventional angiography is the invasive gold standard, requiring vascular puncture and contrast, and is used mainly to guide a planned intervention. It is not where the evaluation of new claudication begins; the bedside ankle-brachial index is. Gold standard does not mean first test.
Computed tomography angiography

Computed tomography angiography uses contrast to delineate arterial anatomy and is used mainly to plan an intervention. For a first evaluation of suspected peripheral artery disease, the simple bedside ankle-brachial index comes first. Contrast studies are for planning, not for initial testing.

set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has had six days of worsening left leg pain and coolness. The limb has no sensory loss or weakness, and imaging shows an arterial thrombus. Which intervention fits this time frame?
opts: Catheter-directed thrombolysis

Correct. Her ischemia has lasted six days, well within the indication for intra-arterial catheter-directed thrombolysis, which is acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days' duration, with alteplase as the thrombolytic drug. With no sensory loss or weakness, her limb is far from the irreversible category that requires amputation.
Major amputation

Major amputation is required for irreversibly ischemic limbs with profound sensory loss and paralysis. Her limb has no sensory loss or weakness after six days, so it is not in that category. Within 14 days, catheter-directed thrombolysis fits the time frame.
Oral aspirin alone

Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent for chronic peripheral artery disease and does not dissolve an arterial thrombus. Her six-day occlusion falls within the under-14-day indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis with alteplase. The question is about the time frame, and only thrombolysis carries one.
Supervised exercise program

Supervised exercise therapy improves walking distance in chronic claudication. A new arterial thrombus causing six days of worsening pain and coolness is acute limb ischemia, and under 14 days it is an indication for catheter-directed thrombolysis. Exercise has no role in acute occlusion.

opts: Computed tomography angiography

Computed tomography angiography is the best diagnostic and pre-intervention planning study, used once repair is being considered. For this asymptomatic smoker with a pulsatile aorta on examination, initial screening uses abdominal ultrasound. Planning comes after screening.
Magnetic resonance imaging

Magnetic resonance imaging is comparable to computed tomography without dye or ionizing radiation and suits stable patients with a dye allergy. He has no allergy, and the first step is screening with abdominal ultrasound. Magnetic resonance is the alternative, not the starting test.
Abdominal ultrasound

Correct. A widened, pulsatile aorta found on routine examination of an asymptomatic 68-year-old smoker calls for screening, and abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic study of choice for initial screening for an aneurysm. It is also used for serial documentation of aneurysm size.
Abdominal X-ray

A plain film shows a calcified outline in only about 75% of aneurysms and misses the 25% that are not calcified. Abdominal ultrasound is the screening study of choice for his suspected aneurysm. A test that misses a quarter of cases cannot screen.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man has had progressive ischemic pain in his right leg for three weeks and is found to have an arterial occlusion. Which intervention falls outside its indication for him?
opts: Arterial bypass procedure

An arterial bypass procedure is one of the surgical therapies for acute peripheral arterial occlusion, and no 14-day limit is attached to it. The only option with a time window is catheter-directed thrombolysis, limited to under 14 days. At three weeks, bypass remains available to him.

Anticoagulation with intravenous heparin is the medical therapy for acute peripheral arterial occlusion and has no stated time limit. The intervention limited to acute limb ischemia of less than 14 days is catheter-directed thrombolysis. Heparin remains appropriate at three weeks.

opts: Large-bore access and emergency surgery

Abdominal ultrasound surveillance

Surveillance ultrasound is for stable, asymptomatic aneurysms followed over months to years. He has severe pain, a pulsatile mass, hypotension and flank ecchymosis from retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which mean rupture, a surgical emergency. Surveillance has no place in an unstable patient.

Pain control is part of managing a symptomatic, unruptured aneurysm, but he is hypotensive with a Grey Turner sign, so the aneurysm has ruptured. A ruptured aneurysm is a surgical emergency needing large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and operation, not observation.
Beta blocker, then elective repair

Beta blockers for blood pressure control, followed by repair, suit a symptomatic but unruptured aneurysm in a stable patient. His pressure of 78/50 and flank ecchymosis mean rupture, and a ruptured aneurysm is a surgical emergency. Hypotension separates rupture from the stable symptomatic case.

set2.q: A 65-year-old man has a painful, swollen right groin two days after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery. Ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall, communicating with the lumen. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Femoral true aneurysm

A true aneurysm involves all three layers of the vessel wall, as a saccular outpouching or a fusiform dilation. His ultrasound shows a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after a femoral puncture, which is a false aneurysm, a pseudoaneurysm. Outside the wall means false.
Acute limb ischemia

Acute limb ischemia is sudden occlusion of a previously patent artery, with a cold, pale, pulseless limb. He has a painful, swollen groin and a blood-filled cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization, which is a pseudoaneurysm. Local swelling, not distal pulselessness, is his problem.
Atheroembolism

Atheroembolism causes painful blue toes from small-vessel debris, usually with palpable pulses. A swollen, painful groin with a cavity outside the arterial wall after catheterization is a pseudoaneurysm. The finding is at the puncture site, not in the toes.
Femoral pseudoaneurysm

Correct. A pseudoaneurysm is a communication between the arterial lumen and overlying connective tissue after arterial rupture, forming a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall. The common site is the femoral artery after cardiac catheterization, from laceration by the access needle, and pain comes from swelling or nerve compression.

set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with known aortic atherosclerosis has sudden pain and tenderness of two toes, which have turned blue. Which pulse finding is expected on examination?
opts: A pulse with a double systolic peak

A double-peaked pulse is not a feature described for limb emboli. With atheroembolism, debris lodges in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable. The expected finding is a preserved pulse despite blue toes.
Distal pulses usually remain palpable

Correct. Sudden painful blue toes with known aortic atherosclerosis point to atheroembolism. The debris of fibrin, platelets and cholesterol tends to lodge in small vessels of muscle and skin and may not occlude large vessels, so distal pulses usually remain palpable.
Pulses absent below the femoral artery

Absent pulses distal to an occlusion are the finding of acute limb ischemia, usually from a thromboembolus blocking a larger artery. Atheroemboli lodge in small vessels and usually leave distal pulses palpable. Blue toes with pulses means small-vessel debris.
Pulses absent in both groins

Absent or diminished femoral pulses point to aortoiliac disease, as in Leriche syndrome with claudication and erectile dysfunction. Atheroemboli to the toes usually come with palpable distal pulses. Her problem is in the digits, not the groins.

set2.q: A 73-year-old man with ischemic rest pain notices that walking around the room eases his foot pain, although walking used to cause calf pain. Which explanation should he be given?
opts: Walking releases natural pain relief

Rest pain is not relieved by a natural pain-relief response; it is poorly controlled even by narcotics. Walking helps him because standing puts the foot in a dependent position, and gravity then aids arterial perfusion, the same effect as hanging the leg over the bed. Position explains the relief.
Walking drains venous blood away

Venous drainage is not the reason. His foot pain eases with walking because standing makes the limb dependent, and gravity helps arterial flow reach the forefoot. Ischemic rest pain is an arterial supply problem, not venous congestion.
Walking lowers his blood pressure

Lower blood pressure would not improve flow to an ischemic foot. The relief comes from dependency: on his feet, gravity aids arterial perfusion, just as hanging the leg over the edge of the bed does. Position, not pressure, explains the paradox.
Dependency uses gravity to aid flow

Correct. Ischemic rest pain is relieved by hanging the leg over the edge of the bed or by walking around. In contrast to claudication, walking around uses the gravity effect of dependence on extremity perfusion, which is why walking that once caused his calf pain now eases his foot.

opts: Refer to supervised exercise rehabilitation

Correct. She should be referred to an exercise rehabilitation program, because a supervised program is more successful than a home-based program. Consistent moderate exercise, at least 30 to 45 minutes three times per week, improves walking distance in stable claudication.
Walk at home; supervision adds nothing

Home walking is not as good: a supervised program is more successful than a home-based program, so the recommendation is referral to exercise rehabilitation. Her question has a direct answer, and it favors supervision.
Refer for bypass graft surgery now

Avoid exercise until pain resolves

Avoiding exercise withholds the therapy that helps: consistent moderate exercise improves walking distance in claudication. She should be referred to a supervised exercise rehabilitation program. Waiting for pain to resolve before walking gets the treatment backward.

Endovascular repair only

Heparin anticoagulates and would work against the thrombosis that seals a pseudoaneurysm. Her 1.4 cm cavity is under 2 cm and may thrombose and regress on its own, so the plan is to watch and wait. The goal here is clot formation, not its prevention.

Venous insufficiency is a differential diagnosis for leg pain, with calf swelling on standing, not a disease coexisting in half of these patients. Coronary artery disease is present in 50% of patients with peripheral artery disease. The stem asks for an associated arterial condition.

opts: Wait until it reaches 5.5 cm

Correct. Evidence of rapid growth, 0.5 cm in six months, means the aneurysm should be repaired. His grew from 4.1 to 4.8 cm, a 0.7 cm increase in six months, so repair is indicated even though 4.8 cm is below the size thresholds of 5.0 cm in women and over 5.5 cm in men.

Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. His is 4.8 cm and grew 0.7 cm in six months, which exceeds the 0.5 cm rapid-growth criterion for repair. Both size and growth rule out the longest interval.
Recheck in 6 to 12 months

set2.q: A 72-year-old man has an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.2 cm, unchanged from last year. Which follow-up is most appropriate?
opts: Elective repair now

At 4.2 cm and unchanged, he is below every repair trigger: 5.0 cm or larger in women, over 5.5 cm in men, or growth of 0.5 cm in six months. He needs surveillance, not surgery. Check both size and growth before choosing repair.
Emergency repair today

Emergency surgery is for a ruptured aneurysm. His is asymptomatic, 4.2 cm and unchanged from last year, so it is followed with imaging every 6 to 12 months. Nothing in the stem suggests rupture or rapid growth.
Imaging every 6 to 12 months

Correct. Surveillance frequency depends on size: an aneurysm of 4.0 to 5.4 cm is imaged with ultrasound or computed tomography every 6 to 12 months. His 4.2 cm aneurysm is asymptomatic and unchanged from last year, so it has no growth trigger for repair.
Ultrasound every three years

Three-yearly ultrasound is for aneurysms of 3.0 to 3.9 cm. At 4.2 cm he has crossed into the 4.0 to 5.4 cm range, which shortens the interval to every 6 to 12 months. Crossing 4.0 cm tightens surveillance.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm is scheduled for elective repair. He asks how the surgeon will choose between endovascular and open repair. Which factor guides the choice?
opts: His age and comorbidities

Correct. Two repair methods exist: endovascular aneurysm repair, a modular graft placed through the iliac or femoral arteries to line the aorta and exclude the sac, and open replacement with a tube or bifurcated prosthetic graft. The choice considers the patient's age and medical comorbidities.
The color of his skin

Skin color plays no part in choosing the repair method. The choice between endovascular and open repair considers his age and medical comorbidities. Race bears on how common aneurysms are, not on how they are repaired.
The result of his ankle index

The ankle-brachial index grades lower extremity arterial disease and does not choose the method of aneurysm repair. Age and medical comorbidities decide between endovascular aneurysm repair and open surgery. A leg test does not settle an aortic decision.
Whether he has a carotid bruit

A carotid bruit relates to carotid artery disease, not the method of aortic repair. The choice between endovascular aneurysm repair and open surgery rests on his age and medical comorbidities. An unrelated examination finding does not drive the decision.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with an acute aortic dissection. His family asks what happens if it is not treated. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Only the legs are at risk

Aortic dissection is a tear in the aorta itself, not a leg problem, and the stakes are much higher. Acute untreated aortic dissection carries a high mortality rate. That is why blood pressure is lowered at once and the diseased aorta is grafted and replaced.
Untreated, mortality is high

Correct. Acute untreated aortic dissection has a high mortality rate. That is why management moves quickly: systolic pressure is reduced to 100 to 120 mmHg with esmolol or nitroprusside, pain is managed, and surgery grafts and replaces the diseased portion of the aorta.
It usually heals by itself

Nothing supports spontaneous healing as the expected course; acute untreated dissection has a high mortality rate. Treatment aims to stop progression by lowering blood pressure, then replace the diseased aorta surgically. A reassuring answer here would mislead the family.
It turns into a pseudoaneurysm

A pseudoaneurysm is a separate lesion, a blood-filled cavity outside the vessel wall, typically after femoral catheterization. The danger of untreated acute dissection is a high mortality rate. The family's question has a blunter answer than a change of lesion type.

set2.q: A 64-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back. Blood pressure is 184/106. Imaging confirms an aortic dissection. Which blood pressure goal applies?
opts: Systolic above 140 mmHg

Keeping systolic pressure above 140 mmHg leaves it too high to stop the dissection's progression. Management reduces systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg with a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside. His 184/106 must come well down.
Systolic below 80 mmHg

A systolic pressure below 80 mmHg is far under the target range and is not the goal. Management reduces systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg to stop progression of the dissection. Overshooting into hypotension is not the aim.
No change until surgery

Leaving his 184/106 untouched until surgery allows the dissection to progress. Management starts immediately by reducing systolic pressure to 100 to 120 mmHg, with pain management, before surgical grafting. Pressure control comes first, not after.
Systolic 100 to 120 mmHg

Correct. Stopping progression of a dissection requires reducing blood pressure, with a systolic goal of 100 to 120 mmHg, using a beta blocker such as esmolol or a vasodilator such as nitroprusside. His pressure of 184/106 is far above that range, and pain management and surgical grafting follow.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man has a 4.8 cm descending thoracic aortic aneurysm, and he now has back pain that is attributed to the aneurysm. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Repair only above 6.0 cm

The over-6.0 cm threshold for descending aneurysms applies to asymptomatic patients. His 4.8 cm aneurysm now causes back pain, and repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms regardless of size. Symptoms override the size threshold.
Repair the aneurysm

Correct. Repair is recommended for all symptomatic thoracic aortic aneurysms. His 4.8 cm descending aneurysm is below the asymptomatic threshold of 6.0 cm, but back pain attributed to the aneurysm makes it symptomatic, and that alone indicates repair.
Imaging every 6 to 12 months

Imaging every 6 to 12 months is surveillance for an asymptomatic 4.5 to 5.4 cm thoracic aneurysm. His 4.8 cm aneurysm now causes back pain, so it is symptomatic, and all symptomatic thoracic aneurysms should be repaired. Symptoms end surveillance.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man has lifestyle-limiting calf claudication despite six months of supervised exercise and antiplatelet therapy, and revascularization is being planned. Which study is the gold standard for defining his arterial anatomy?
opts: Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is a simple bedside test that grades severity, but it does not map arterial anatomy. For revascularization planning, the gold standard is conventional angiography. A pressure ratio cannot show where to intervene.
Pulse volume recording

Pulse volume recording is not among the studies listed for defining arterial anatomy before an intervention. Those are computed tomography angiography, magnetic resonance angiography and conventional angiography, with conventional angiography the gold standard. Choose the study named as most accurate and informative.
Conventional angiography

Correct. Conventional angiography is the gold standard and the most accurate and informative test. It is invasive, requiring vascular puncture with catheters placed at the stenosis and contrast injected, and it is used primarily for guidance when an intervention, like his planned revascularization, is planned.
Duplex ultrasound

Duplex ultrasound is the mainstay initial noninvasive imaging when stenosis is suspected, needing no contrast or radiation, but it is not the gold standard. Conventional angiography is the most accurate and informative test for anatomy before an intervention. Initial noninvasive is not the same as gold standard.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man is scheduled for a femoral-popliteal bypass graft using his saphenous vein. He asks what can go wrong. Which complications should he be counseled about?
opts: Kidney stones and gout flares

Kidney stones and gout are not listed complications of bypass surgery. The complications of a bypass graft are myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. Counsel on the cardiovascular and graft risks.
Heart attack, stroke, graft infection

Correct. Bypass graft surgery, here a femoral-popliteal bypass with his saphenous vein, is invasive and highly effective, but its complications include myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. These are what he should be counseled about.
Hoarseness and difficulty swallowing

Hoarseness and dysphagia are compression symptoms of thoracic aortic aneurysms of the arch and descending aorta, not risks of a leg bypass. His counseling should cover myocardial infarction, stroke, graft infection and peripheral embolization. Match symptoms to the anatomy involved.
Heart block needing a pacemaker

Heart block is not among the listed bypass complications. The named risks are myocardial infarction and stroke, infection of the graft and peripheral embolization. A cardiac complication does appear, but it is infarction, not a conduction problem.
